content: 1. Resources should be utilized effectively, and lessons learned from other integrated disease prevention and control initiatives should be applied. It is essential to monitor the execution and progress of these efforts and to establish accountability for actions taken. 2. Critical partners must be engaged and embedded into the overall work plan and approach. This includes involving other programs and sectors, engaging the private sector and non-governmental organizations, and collaborating with United Nations agencies and development partners. 3. Innovations should be promoted, particularly those that address barriers to service delivery. Efforts must be made to generate demand for services while ensuring adequate supply. Implementation research should focus on identifying optimal delivery methods for existing interventions to reach the most vulnerable populations. 4. The targets outlined in the Integrated Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Pneumonia and Diarrhea (GAPPD) cannot be achieved without urgent action from national governments and global partners. Coordinated and integrated international, national, and sub-national actions are required to sustain and enhance progress in reducing child mortality. 5. This document calls on all stakeholders to demonstrate their commitment, allocate necessary resources, and collaborate to eliminate preventable child deaths caused by pneumonia and diarrhea, making such tragedies a thing of the past. 6. The GAPPD proposes a cohesive approach to ending preventable deaths from pneumonia and diarrhea. It integrates critical services and interventions to create healthy environments, promote protective practices, and ensure access to proven preventive and treatment measures for every child. 7. Achieving universal coverage will require scaling up and targeting interventions known to prevent and control pneumonia and diarrhea. This will be accomplished through coordinated and collaborative child health programs. 8. Parents, communities, community health workers, civil society, and the private sector all play significant roles in realizing this vision. Clear goals and coverage targets have been established to reduce morbidity and mortality from pneumonia and diarrhea by 2015, within the context of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). 9. Despite significant progress, much more can be achieved through accelerated action. The United Nations Global Strategy for Women’s and Children’s Health, launched in 2010, emphasizes a continuum of care approach to save lives, aiming to reduce child mortality to 20 or fewer deaths per 1,000 live births in every country by 2035. 10. Revised goals for 2025 include reducing pneumonia mortality in children under five to fewer than 3 per 1,000 live births, reducing diarrhea mortality to fewer than 1 per 1,000 live births, and reducing the incidence of severe pneumonia and diarrhea by 75% compared to 2010 levels. Additionally, the global prevalence of stunting in children under five should be reduced by 40%. 11. These ambitious goals require significant political will and additional resource mobilization. Coverage targets include achieving 90% full-dose vaccine coverage, 90% access to appropriate case management for pneumonia and diarrhea, and at least 50% exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months of life by 2025. 12. By 2030, universal access to basic drinking water in healthcare facilities and homes, adequate sanitation in healthcare facilities, and handwashing facilities with water and soap must be achieved. Universal access to clean and safe energy technologies in healthcare facilities and homes is also a priority. 13. Progress toward these targets will be measured through national health information systems, demographic and health surveys, and research efforts. The United Nations Commission on Information and Accountability and the independent Expert Review Group will play key roles in monitoring and evaluation. 14. Pneumonia and diarrhea remain leading causes of child mortality, accounting for 29% of all child deaths globally. These diseases disproportionately affect children in the poorest regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, where nearly 90% of deaths occur. 15. Proven interventions exist to prevent and treat pneumonia and diarrhea, but services are often fragmented, and those most at risk are not being reached. Addressing these diseases in an integrated manner strengthens weak health systems and ensures more effective delivery of interventions. 16. The GAPPD provides an integrated framework of key interventions to protect, prevent, and treat pneumonia and diarrhea in children under five. It identifies opportunities to better integrate activities, capture synergies, and improve the efficiency of resource use. 17. The GAPPD builds on existing initiatives, such as the Global Strategy for Women’s and Children’s Health, the United Nations Commission on Life-Saving Commodities, and the 2012 Declaration on Scaling Up Treatment of Diarrhea and Pneumonia. These initiatives aim to mobilize political leadership, improve service delivery, and ensure accountability. 18. The solutions to tackling pneumonia and diarrhea do not require major technological advances. Proven interventions are available, and millions of young lives can be saved by providing these interventions at levels already achieved in better-off households. 19. The GAPPD emphasizes the importance of evidence-based country plans, transparency, and global communication to drive collective action and achieve its goals. It calls on all stakeholders to prioritize pneumonia and diarrhea control as part of national health strategies.
